analysis.one_liner: Boosts antitrust enforcement against hospital mergers and forces hospitals to publish real prices.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 2020 with one cosponsor, the bill was referred to three House committees and died without a hearing or vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would fund federal antitrust investigations of hospital mergers, require hospitals in highly concentrated markets to accept Medicare Advantage-level payment rates from all payers, and force hospitals to post the volume-weighted average prices they charge for the 100 most common shoppable services. It would also ban contract terms that stop insurers from steering patients to cheaper, higher-quality providers, protect patients from bills based on wrong provider-directory information, require itemized bills within 45 days, and fund a national database of health care claims to show what care actually costs. It was never taken up by any committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and employers who pay hospital prices. The bill funds antitrust enforcement against hospital consolidation, requires concentrated hospital systems to accept Medicare Advantage-level rates from all payers, publishes what hospitals actually charge for common services, bans gag clauses and all-or-nothing contract terms that hide price and quality information from plans and enrollees, reimburses patients who are billed out-of-network rates after relying on a wrong provider directory, requires itemized bills within 45 days of a visit, and funds a national claims database showing the cost and quality of care. States without certificate-of-need laws and with broadened scope of practice for nurse practitioners and physician assistants would qualify for $1 billion a year in infrastructure grants [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $160 million for the Federal Trade Commission to hire staff to investigate anti-competitive mergers and practices by providers of inpatient and outpatient health care, and extends the FTC's antitrust authority to tax-exempt (nonprofit) hospital organizations.

Requires hospitals in counties with population density above the median that sit in markets with a concentration index (HHI) above 4,000 to apply their average Medicare Advantage reimbursement rate to all patients, with exemptions for rural hospitals and those with under 15% regional market share.

Requires hospitals to publicly post, in a standardized federal digital system, the volume-weighted average price they charge for each of the 100 most commonly shoppable hospital services, beginning in 2021.

Prohibits health plans from agreeing to contract terms that restrict sharing provider-specific price and quality information with enrollees, and bans terms that stop plans from steering patients to lower-cost providers or that force plans to contract with every hospital affiliate.

Requires plans to verify provider directory information every 90 days, and requires providers to reimburse patients the full amount above in-network cost-sharing, plus interest, if the patient was billed out-of-network rates after relying on incorrect directory information.

Requires facilities to give patients a list of services rendered within 5 days of a visit and adjudicated bills within 45 days, with civil monetary penalties up to $10,000 per violation for repeat offenders, and requires providers to give a good-faith cost-sharing estimate within 2 business days of a request.

Contracts with at least two nonprofit entities to build a national database of medical, prescription drug, and payment claims, with public reports on price, utilization, and spending trends, and authorizes $20 million to start it plus $15 million a year through 2025.

Authorizes $1 billion per year from 2021 through 2030 in hospital infrastructure grants to states that have no certificate-of-need law, allow nurse practitioners and physician assistants to evaluate, diagnose, and treat patients, have no anti-steering network laws, and have no Certificate of Public Advantage laws that displace competition.

analysis.who_pays: Consolidated hospital systems would bear the largest costs: site-neutral Medicare payment for off-campus provider-based departments, Medicare Advantage-level rates in concentrated urban markets, FTC merger scrutiny reaching their nonprofit systems, and mandatory price publication. Taxpayers would fund the FTC staffing, the $1 billion-a-year state grants, and the claims database. Health insurers gain negotiating leverage against hospitals, and physician investors gain from the repeal of Affordable Care Act limits on physician-owned hospital expansion.

drawbacks.text: Raises Medicare cost-based reimbursement for critical access hospitals from 101% to 102% in 2021, rising one percentage point a year to 110% after 2029, which increases federal Medicare spending to keep rural hospitals afloat.

Repeals the Affordable Care Act provisions (Section 6001) that restrict the expansion of physician-owned hospitals, restoring those rules as if they had never been enacted, which would let physician-investors open and expand facilities that doctors own and refer to.

Creates a new antitrust exemption allowing private health insurers to jointly negotiate hospital prices with each other, a safe harbor for coordinated insurer bargaining power whose savings for patients are not guaranteed to be passed through to premiums.

Conditions hospital infrastructure grants on states not having certificate-of-need laws, but also on states not having network adequacy laws regulating insurer networks, which could reward states for dropping protections that guarantee patients reasonable access to in-network primary and specialty care.

Eliminates eligibility for certain types of Medicare accountable care organizations by striking three paragraphs of the ACO statute, ending shared-savings arrangements that some providers and patients currently participate in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — funded antitrust enforcement, mandatory price publication, contract and gag-clause bans, directory accuracy with reimbursement, timely itemized bills, and a public claims database — is aimed squarely at lowering hospital prices and giving patients and employers usable information, and the strongest provisions have real teeth. But the bill is also a package of trade-offs: it raises rural hospital Medicare rates and costs, reopens physician-owned hospital expansion despite well-documented concerns that physician ownership steers profitable referrals, and hands insurers a collective-bargaining exemption whose benefits to consumers are less certain. On balance it is a serious pro-competition bill with expensive sweeteners, not a clean one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever held a hearing or sent it to the floor, and it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Banks (R-IN) introduced the Hospital Competition Act of 2020 on August 25, 2020, near the end of the 116th Congress.
On the day of introduction it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, additionally, to the Ways and Means and Judiciary Committees, splitting jurisdiction three ways.
One Republican joined as a cosponsor; no Democrat did.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral; the Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consolidated hospital systems, whose pricing power, merger freedom, and site-based Medicare payments stayed untouched; insurers also kept the status quo negotiating rules. Patients gained nothing because none of the transparency, antitrust, or billing protections took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consolidated hospital systems kept the status quo

industries.industry: Consolidated hospital systems and hospital operators
industries.note: The bill cuts their Medicare revenue through site-neutral payment and Medicare Advantage-level rates in concentrated urban markets, subjects their nonprofit parents to FTC merger scrutiny for the first time, and forces publication of the prices they charge for common services. These losses are the mechanism by which patients would pay less.

Insurers gain leverage against hospitals: a new antitrust exemption to jointly negotiate hospital prices, bans on gag clauses and all-or-nothing affiliate contracting, and access to claims data. Whether that leverage translates into lower premiums for patients is not guaranteed by the bill.

They are exempted from the concentrated-market rate requirement and get their Medicare cost reimbursement raised up to 110% over a decade, plus a share of $1 billion-a-year infrastructure grants. This keeps rural hospitals open, though at higher cost to Medicare and taxpayers.

The bill repeals the Affordable Care Act restrictions on physician-owned hospital expansion, letting physician-investors build and expand facilities they own and refer to. Supporters frame this as competition; critics note it reopens a referral channel Congress restricted in 2010.

Employers get access to de-identified claims data, customized cost reports, and contracts free of gag clauses, letting them compare prices and design networks. This lowers their health spending but is not an industry interest running against patients.

Health plans must report the 50 most dispensed, most costly, and fastest-rising drugs and disclose rebate and other remuneration from manufacturers, aggregated so no single drug or plan is named. The exposure is limited but creates a public record of where drug money flows.
